>
> Hi,
>
> First of all, congrats for the great package! From what I've seen, it has a lot of useful and standard tools for DES. Having this open-source option is a great deal!

Thanks! :)

> Anyway, I've been trying to model an inventory system with simmer by using a trajectory as a general definition for any demand arrival, irrespective of the place where demand arrives, so I need to keep track of the inventory in many "locations" using one single trajectory. For that I was thinking on using an array (in this case a matrix) that keeps track of every inventory position, depending on the location where the demand arrived. The issue is that I haven't been able to change the value of an "external" array by calling an "external" function, as it seems that the simulation does not interact with these external definitions.
>
> I've seen that simmer allows to set a global variable for the simulation, but this variable is only numeric and it cannot work as an array/matrix. I need to use an array/matrix because I want the simulation to be flexible so I can use one single trajectory to define the same tasks but with different "locations"; otherwise, if I have, for example, a 100 location network, then I would need to define 100 different trajectories and/or global variables. Does anyone have any idea how can I accomplish this?

In short, use <<- instead of <-.

Long explanation follows. When you use a variable, there's a search
through parent environments until there's a match (in your case, in
the global environment). Instead, when you try to change a variable,
operators <- and = assign into the environment in which they are
evaluated. This means that, regardless there's a variable with the
same name in the global environment, a new one is created locally. You
need to use <<- to force that same search across environment
boundaries and modify the global one.

Iñaki

a question for you though:

t1 <- trajectory() %>%
  rollback_point("foo")

t3 <- join(t1, t2)

What would you expect here? Of course, I have an opinion already, but

About loops, I can't think of any more generic way of doing them
beyond a simple jump condition (as the rollback is; and the idea above
about labelling returning points will definitely improve its
usability), but suggestions are welcome.

On the other hand, I don't think that joining or branching inexistent
trajectories is a good idea. It requires NSE magic that complicates
things unnecessarily and breaks stuff. What you can already do is the
following:

t1 <- trajectory() %>%
  seize("something") %>%
  branch(function() 0, continue=TRUE) %>%
  release("something")

option1 <- trajectory() %>%
  timeout(1)
option2 <- trajectory() %>%
  timeout(2)

t1[2] <- trajectory() %>%
  branch(function() sample(2, 1), continue=c(TRUE, TRUE), option1, option2)

Note that it doesn't even need to be a branch (the first placeholder
in the definition of t1, I mean), because you can substitute any
activity with any other, as if trajectories were lists (they are in
some sense).

> Is there any way to avoid this behaviour?

Not at the moment. Reneging activities return all the resources held,
because they are, in principle, designed to completely leave the
system. But I can see the value of just releasing the one in which the
arrival is enqueued. I'll open an issue to track this feature request.

In the meantime, as a workaround, you can

- seize resource A
- decrease capacity of resource A
- release resource A
- set renege_in
- seize resource B (enqueued)
...
- increase capacity of resource A (when you want to release A)

In this way, if reneging is triggered, the arrival still effectively
has resource A seized, because you didn't increase the capacity yet.
You have to take this into account in your analyses though.

> > >> This is an excellent idea, and shouldn't be hard to implement. I have
> > >> a question for you though:
> > >>
> > >> t1 <- trajectory() %>%
> > >>   rollback_point("foo")
> > >> t2 <- trajectory() %>%
> > >>   rollback("foo")
> > >> t3 <- join(t1, t2)
> > >>
> > >> What would you expect here? Of course, I have an opinion already, but
> > >> I don't want to bias your expectations. ;-)
> > > I'd expect the rollback in t3 to roll back to the rollback point in t3 - I think the names will have to be global in scope (as far as trajectories are concerned)
> >
> > Ok. And now, ignore t1 and t3. What would you expect if you insert an arrival into t2?
> >
> > I guess that given my assertion they should be global in scope, the arrival should end up in t1. The only logical alternative I can see is to throw an error that there's no "foo" in this trajectory, which seems less useful.
>
> No, it shouldn't cross independent trajectories, because otherwise the behaviour is undefined if there are multiple definitions of the same label.
>
> It should go backwards in the trajectory until the first matching label is found. The question is what happens if no proper label is found. The options are:

If they were global you could throw an error when if a label is repeated. Having them local to a trajectory is equally valid but presumably you'll want to throw an error when:

t1 <- trajectory() %>%
 rollback_point("foo")

t2 <- trajectory() %>%

 rollback_point("foo")

t3<- join(t1,t2) %>%
 rollback("foo")

Unless you define that it will always roll back to the first, or last, or most recent point (but even then I think a warning would be advisable)

 With rollbacks scoped to trajectories - in terms of what to do when the only matching rollback point is in a different trajectory or non-existent, I'd vote for throwing an error (option 3) as first choice, rolling to top of the trajectory with a warning (option 1) as second choice. Option 2 seems to fail the principle of least surprise, to me.

tom

messages.body_plain:
Dear all, dear Iñaki

My questoin is very basic towards DES, but I've gone through the simmer examples and I was reading through this newsgroup, but I'm struggling with a conceptional problem and I hope, you tell me it's a stupid question, because easily solvable :)

I would like to build a simulator for electric cars at charging stations, but not like in the gas station example, where multiple cars queue up. In my scenario, every car has its dedicated charger, but cars have to share a common maximum power (P_max). The chargers have to make sure that the sum of all chargers' power output never exceeds P_max.

This means the chargers in the simulation would have to adjust the power output depending on the demand of other cars. Lower power output means longer charging time. Sometimes cars would leave before they are fully charged, which would free resources to give more power to the remaining cars, shortening again the charging duration of the remaining cars.

To determine when cars are arriving or leaving, I have a dataset of real cars that I recorded when they arrive and leave. The generator would randomly sample from this dataset.

In my first simulation attempt, I tried to stick to the gas station example. Problem: When a car seizes a charger, I don't know the power with which it can charge, because it depends on the other chargers. How do I implement/resolve these dependencies among objects? Would you signal at every time slot what each charger demands and negotiate the sharing in a separate function?

As I didn't find a solution by myself, I tried to turn the logic around and make a generator of energy (based on P_max). The energy objects queue for cars to be charged. the cars would then be elements to seize, which appear and disappear depending on my recorded schedules. But I didn't find out how to count how much "energy" has been consumed, to model that the battery inside the car is full (stop charging) - or how to know when the car leaves before it was fully charged, how full the battery actually was.

Do you see a way how to realize this simulation with simmer?

I don't see the power either as a resource or as a process, but as an overall constraint. In my view, there's a station with capacity equal to N chargers; cars arrive, stay for some time and leave. When a particular car arrives, it seizes one charger, and calculates (and saves this as an attribute) its power share as the minimum between its maximum input power and the total power divided by the number of chargers seized (get_server_count). The timeout can be derived from this power and the battery size. Finally, the power attribute changes to zero and the car releases the charger.

Now, every time a car arrives, it must send a signal to notify all the existing cars that they need to recompute their input power and the remaining timeout (based on the battery status and the new power). The following vignette is relevant here: https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-04-bank-2.html#interrupting-a-process

At the end of the simulation, the attribute table will have the charging profile for each car, as in this vignette: https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-aa-5g#energy-efficiency-for-massive-iot

Regards,
Iñaki

messages.body_plain:
First, let me begin by thanking the developers for the impressive work they have done. I can think of nothing that I used to do using commercial software that I cannot do using Simmer.

I am trying to reduce the number of attributes used in a simulation. There is a set of 6 attributes that may or may not be used before the simulated patient leaves the model. These attributes are patient-specific treatment effects; thus, they must be set as the patient enters the model. When simulating 100,000 patients and repeating this simulation 1,000 times while varying key parameters, then updating a set of 6 variables/cells in the global environment and reading from them when needed (I think) will be of great advantage.

I understand that I could just use global attributes. However, because these 6 attributes are called when a patient switches treatment, using global attributes the code will be rigid (hardcoded) compared to using a matrix/dataframe/tibble.

To give a simple example of what I want to achieve:
rm(list = ls())

library(simmer)

env = simmer()

global_var = 0

entry = trajectory() %>%

  set_attribute(keys = "test", values = function() rnorm(1)) %>%

  global_var = get_attribute(env, "test") * age^2

env %>%

  add_generator("tests", entry, function() 1, mon = 2)

Any help will be appreciated, thank you.
